title: Narrative tenses mastery
note: past perfect for the earlier event and for a result already true in the scene · past perfect continuous vs past perfect (how long vs how much), state verbs excluded · past continuous background against past simple events · narrative control: used to / would for habit, and when past perfect should be LEFT OUT · 4 strands x 12 · 48 items · first C1 unit, built to live 2026-08-07 (cloud run 10)

items.en: The streets were empty; it had stopped raining.
items.cz: Ulice byly prázdné; přestalo pršet.
items.gap: The streets were empty; it ____ raining.
accepts: The streets were empty; it had stopped raining.
items.explanation: Past perfect marks the event that happened first, or a result that was already true in the past scene. The verb carrying the story stays in past simple.
items.explanation_cz: Předminulý čas označuje děj, který se stal dřív, nebo výsledek, který v minulé scéně už platil. Sloveso, které nese příběh, zůstává v past simple.

items.explanation: Past perfect continuous stresses how long the process ran; past perfect stresses that it was finished or how much was done. State verbs (know, be, live as a state) take the simple form.
items.explanation_cz: Předminulý průběhový zdůrazňuje, jak dlouho proces běžel; předminulý prostý zdůrazňuje, že byl dokončen, nebo kolik se toho udělalo. Stavová slovesa (know, be, live ve významu stavu) mají tvar prostý.

items.explanation: Past continuous paints the background — what was already going on when the scene opens. Past simple gives the events that move the story forward and cut into that background.
items.explanation_cz: Průběhový minulý čas maluje pozadí — co už probíhalo, když scéna začíná. Prostý minulý čas přináší děje, které příběh posouvají dál a do toho pozadí zasáhnou.

items.explanation: used to and would both give repeated past habit, but would needs an action verb, never a state. And when after, before or a plain sequence already makes the order clear, the past perfect is optional — leaving it out is usually better style.
items.explanation_cz: used to i would vyjadřují opakovaný zvyk v minulosti, would ale potřebuje sloveso činnosti, nikdy stav. A když pořadí už jasně určuje after, before nebo prostá posloupnost, je předminulý čas volitelný — vynechat ho bývá stylisticky lepší.

cards.title: Narrative control, not new tenses
cards.body: You already have every past form. The C1 skill is choosing which combination builds the story — and knowing when the plain past simple is the better choice.
cards.body_cz: Všechny minulé tvary už umíte. Dovednost na úrovni C1 je vybrat, která kombinace staví příběh — a poznat, kdy je lepší prostý minulý čas.

table.caption: the four layers
rows: main events
past simple
He opened the door and sat down.
background
past continuous
The sun was shining.
earlier past
past perfect
The train had already left.
earlier process
past perfect continuous
She had been waiting for an hour.

points: One scene usually needs three of these, not one.

cards.title: Past perfect is a signal, not a rule
cards.title_cz: Předminulý čas je signál, ne povinnost
cards.body: Past perfect exists to show that one event came before another when the order is not otherwise clear. If after, before or the plain order of the sentence already says it, you do not need it.
cards.body_cz: Předminulý čas ukazuje, že jeden děj předcházel druhému, když to pořadí jinak není jasné. Pokud to už říká after, before nebo prosté pořadí ve větě, potřeba není.
points: Needed: When I got to the station, the train had already left.
Not needed: After we finished dinner, we watched a film.
Not needed: He opened the door, walked in and sat down.
Overusing it makes writing heavy — that is the commonest C1 fault here.

cards.title: How long, or how much?
cards.body: Past perfect continuous answers how long the process ran. Past perfect answers whether it was finished, or how much got done.
cards.body_cz: Předminulý průběhový odpovídá na to, jak dlouho proces běžel. Předminulý prostý na to, jestli byl dokončen, nebo kolik se toho udělalo.

table.caption: the pair
rows: She had been writing all morning.
She had written three reports.
We had been driving for six hours.
We had driven four hundred kilometres.
He had been working in the garden. (so his hands were dirty)
He had finished the garden. (so it looked good)

points: State verbs have no continuous: They had known each other for years, never `had been knowing`.
The continuous often explains a visible state: Her eyes were red; she had been crying.

cards.title: used to and would
cards.body: Both give a repeated habit in the past that is over. would is the more literary of the two and takes only action verbs — a state needs used to.
cards.body_cz: Obojí vyjadřuje opakovaný zvyk v minulosti, který už skončil. would je z těch dvou literárnější a pojí se jen se slovesy činnosti — u stavu je nutné used to.
points: Every Sunday we would walk to the park. (action — both work)
We used to live in a small village. (state — only used to)
Never `would live` for a state, and never `was used to` for a habit — that means something else: accustomed to.
Negative and question drop the -d: He did not use to like his job.

cards.title: Common mistakes

table.caption: check
rows: They had been knowing each other for years.
They had known each other for years.
After we had finished dinner, we had watched a film.
After we finished dinner, we watched a film.
He would live in a small village.
He used to live in a small village.
He did not used to like his job.
He did not use to like his job.
While he spoke, someone knocked.
While he was speaking, someone knocked.
I was going to call her, but she already left.
I was going to call her, but she had already left.

points: Czech has one past tense, so the layers must be built from meaning, not translated.
was used to + -ing = accustomed; used to + infinitive = a former habit.
